newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS - Swedish forestry groups paint dull picture.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Swedish forestry groups paint dull picture.

text.p: Swedish forestry companies have given little hope of a pick-up in the sector with the four major players reporting sharply lower profits in 1996 due to continuing low prices, analysts said on Thursday.

AssiDoman, which on Thursday posted a 61 percent slump in 1996 profits, was the one of the pack that made the most optimistic noises for 1997 but all seemed uncertain about the market's direction in the short term.
Analysts were sceptical about AssiDoman's forecasts for pulp prices to bottom in the first half of 1997 and for a gradual improvement in the business cycle during the year.
"Really 1997 is already a lost year," an analyst from Skandiabanken told Reuters.
"I don't think profits will be much changed from 1996 levels. But 1998 will be better."
Falling pulp and paper prices have taken a heavy toll on Sweden's forestry sectors.
The only saving grace to counteract the slump in prices for some companies was currency hedging.
MoDo, which reported at 44 percent drop in 1996 net profits, said hedging lifted its profits by 1.45 billion in 1996. It posted a profit after financial items of 2.92 billion crowns.
"But they won't even have this to fall back on in 1997 so in some cases we could see even lower profits," said a London based forestry analyst
AssiDoman's comments about pulp prices hitting bottom in the first half of 1997 were treated sceptically.
Hopes of a price rise have been undermined by increases in investories over the northern hemisphere winter months.

"If there is a pick up in economic growth then pulp prices probably won't sink to much below $500 a tonnes but we need to see more demand, particularly from the Far East, to take up the excess capacity in the pulp industry," one analyst said.
Analyst Claes Vikbladh from Ohman was a bit more optimistic, expecting some increases by the year end.
"But I think it's important to point out that we're looking at is a very slow upturn in pulp prices," Vikbladh said.
Analysts said it was hard to see what more the forestry companies themselves could do to save the sitution.
Forestry groups are very dependent on the economic climate.
"Unfortunately for these companies they're at the mercy of what happens at the macro level and they cannot be expected to know what will happen. They can just hope," said one analyst.

"SCA has managed to make cuts but companies like AssiDoman really don't have the room to do that. The sector is going to get more competitive this year with companies looking to improve their own performance internally."
SCA (Svenska Cellulosa Aktiebolaget), Sweden's largest forestry company, reported 1996 profits fell 38 percent to 3.57 billion crowns, hurt by lower prices and slack demand.
The fourth key player, Stora, said 1996 profits plummeted to 2.35 billion crowns from 8.02 billion. The company blamed a weak economic trend in Europe.
However analyst Mads Asprem from Morgan Stanley said it was positive to see three of the forestry companies proposing higher dividends. Only Stora left its unchanged.
"This shows they intend to maintain payments and it is a good sign for shareholders," Asprem said.
